passage:
I share a pod with Trisha at the analytics firm. Last Wednesday she was furious. "Varun keeps copying the director on everything. He's trying to take credit for the dashboard. I know it."
Then she did something I've rarely seen anyone do. She stopped mid-sentence, stared into her coffee, and said, "Hang on. Do I want the director to see my name?" A pause. "Yes. I really do." She laughed a little, and the anger just went out of her.
The next morning she asked our manager if she could present the dashboard at the Friday review. Varun helped her set up the slides.
I can't say what went on inside her. But I've started trying that pause myself.
— Ojas

qa.q: What did Trisha ask the manager the next morning?
qa.a: If she could present the dashboard at the Friday review.

qa.q: Why did Trisha feel so sure Varun was out to take credit?
qa.a: Trisha wanted the director to notice her own work, and that unspoken wish made Varun's emails look like a grab for credit.

qa.q: What turning point took the heat out of Trisha's anger?
qa.a: Pausing to ask whether she wanted the same thing, and admitting she did, showed the real need, to be seen, which she could then ask for directly.

qa.q: How might Varun have experienced that week?
qa.a: Varun may never have known he was suspected, and simply ended up helping Trisha set up her slides.

grounding: A colleague watches a young analyst, sure a teammate is stealing credit, stop to ask whether she wants the same thing and then ask for what she needs.

Day one. Lalremsiami read Shalini's message in the family group, "Maybe we should all decide the Christmas menu together?", and felt her jaw lock. She's trying to take over, she thought. She wants to run everything.
Day three. Writing in her notebook at night, Lalremsiami asked herself an odd question: is there any part of me that wants to run everything? The pen stopped. Yes. She had planned the menu alone for four years and loved being the one who did it. She wrote: I want my effort to be seen.
Day seven. She called Shalini. "I'd love help with the sweets. And I'd love it if people knew I did the rest."
Shalini laughed. "Deal. You're head chef."

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami write in her notebook?
qa.a: I want my effort to be seen.

qa.q: Why did Shalini's message feel like a takeover to Lalremsiami?
qa.a: Lalremsiami loved being the one in charge of the menu, and that same wish to run things made Shalini's suggestion look like a grab for control.

qa.q: What choice on day three changed how Lalremsiami felt?
qa.a: Asking herself whether she also wanted to run everything, and writing down her real need, cooled the anger and showed her what to ask for.

qa.q: How might Shalini have felt receiving Lalremsiami's call?
qa.a: Shalini was probably relieved to be welcomed in to help, and happy to hand Lalremsiami the head-chef title 😊

grounding: Over a week a young woman sure a relative wants to take over pauses to find the same wish in herself, and names what she needs.

passage:
Bhavna, you think your new neighbour looks down on you? Let your Minakshi aunty tell you something from when I was twenty-five.
We had just moved to Nagpur. The woman next door, Mrs Kale, never smiled at me. I was certain she thought I was beneath her, with her polished brass and her kitchen always full of guests. I used to shut my door a little louder, just so she'd hear.
One night, with my hand on that door, I stopped and asked myself: am I the one looking down? I sat with it. Yes. I thought she was showy. And under that, I envied her full kitchen. I was lonely.
The next Sunday I took her some poha. She was shy, not proud. We were friends for thirty years.

qa.q: What did Minakshi take to Mrs Kale the next Sunday?
qa.a: Some poha.

qa.q: Why was young Minakshi so certain Mrs Kale looked down on her?
qa.a: Minakshi was quietly judging Mrs Kale as showy and envying her full kitchen, so she saw that same looking-down in her neighbour.

qa.q: What turning point came with Minakshi's hand on the door?
qa.a: She stopped to ask whether she was the one looking down, which uncovered her loneliness and led her to reach out with poha.

qa.q: How might Mrs Kale have seen the young woman next door who shut her door so loudly?
qa.a: Being shy, Mrs Kale may have thought the newcomer was cross or unfriendly, and felt too awkward to smile first.

grounding: An aunt recalls how, at twenty-five, she stopped to ask whether her neighbour's supposed contempt was her own, and found loneliness underneath.

passage:
The site office in Thane had no power, rain drummed on the tin roof, and Suraj's phone showed four percent. He opened one email and went cold. Wasim, his partner in their two-person design studio, had written to the client directly, without copying him. He's cutting me out, Suraj thought. He wants the whole project for himself. He started typing, "So this is how you work?"
Then he stopped, thumb hovering. Last Friday he had sent the client a sketch on his own, secretly hoping they would see him as the real lead. The heat drained out of his chest. He didn't need to catch Wasim out. He needed to know his place in the studio was safe.
He deleted the line and wrote: "Can we fix who emails the client? I think we both want credit. Call tonight?" He hit send as the screen went black.

qa.q: What did Wasim do that made Suraj go cold?
qa.a: Wasim had written to the client directly, without copying Suraj.

qa.q: Why did Suraj feel so sure that Wasim was trying to cut him out?
qa.a: Suraj had secretly done the same thing last Friday, hoping to be seen as the lead, so that motive felt obvious to him; he was reading his own wish into Wasim's email.

qa.q: What choice, while Suraj's thumb hovered, changed how things went?
qa.a: Suraj stopped before sending the angry line and asked whether he had done the same; that turned an accusation into a practical request about who emails the client and how credit is shared.

qa.q: How might Wasim have felt if "So this is how you work?" had been sent instead?
qa.a: Wasim would likely have felt accused without knowing why and might have defended himself, so the real question about shared credit would never have come up.

grounding: Shows an adult, certain of a partner's bad motives, pausing to find the same impulse in himself, which cools the anger and reveals his real need for a secure place.

passage:
At the Kochi branch, Ankita kept leaning over Francis's desk. "Want me to run those loan files through my checklist? It's quicker." Each time, Francis smiled tightly. She wants to make me look slow before appraisals, he told himself. She's showing off for the manager.
On the ferry home, the certainty sat in his throat. He watched the water and asked a harder question: would I do that? The honest answer stung. For months he had kept his own shortcuts to himself, hoping to shine a little brighter than her in the review.
Saying it, even silently, made it smaller. Underneath the anger was something plainer: he felt behind, and he wanted to be good at this job.
The next morning he rolled his chair over. "Ankita, show me that checklist? And I'll show you how I sort the old files."

qa.q: Where did Francis ask himself the harder question?
qa.a: On the ferry home, while he watched the water.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling underneath his suspicion of Ankita?
qa.a: Underneath the anger, Francis felt behind and insecure, because he had been quietly competing with her himself by keeping his shortcuts secret.

qa.q: What turning point let Francis move from suspicion to something useful?
qa.a: Admitting that he carried the same wish to outshine her; once named, it showed he felt behind and wanted to improve, so he asked to learn her checklist and offered his own method in return.

qa.q: What might the next morning have been like for Ankita when Francis rolled his chair over?
qa.a: After weeks of tight smiles, Ankita might feel relieved and welcomed, since her offers were finally met with interest and a fair swap instead of coldness 🙂

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who checks his hot certainty about a colleague's motives against his own competitive impulse and discovers his actual need to feel capable.

"Vikas, I'm telling you, Dev is trying to steal the Mehta project from me."
"Steal it how?"
"He keeps cc-ing the manager on every email. He wants her to think it was all him."
Vikas stirred his tea at the stall outside the office. "Did he say anything like that?"
"He doesn't need to. I just know."
"Okay. Can I ask you something weird?"
"What?"
"Have you thought about cc-ing her too?"
Pranav opened his mouth. Then shut it. "...Yes. All week, actually."
"So?"
Pranav stared at the traffic. "So maybe I'm the one who wants her to think it was me." He laughed, a bit embarrassed. "I just want her to see my part. She's never mentioned it once."
"Then tell her that. Straight. Not through Dev."
Pranav nodded slowly. The heat in his chest had gone.

qa.q: Where were Pranav and Vikas drinking tea?
qa.a: At the stall outside the office.

qa.q: Why did the heat in Pranav's chest go away?
qa.a: Once Pranav admitted wanting the manager to notice his own part, he felt relieved and a bit embarrassed, and his certainty about Dev's bad motives lost its force.

qa.q: What does Pranav actually need, and how can he get it?
qa.a: He needs his manager to see his work; he can tell her directly what he did instead of fighting Dev.

qa.q: How might Dev see the cc-ing if you asked him?
qa.a: Dev might simply see it as keeping the manager informed, with no plan to steal anything.

grounding: Shows an adult certain of a colleague's bad motives pausing to find the same impulse in himself, which cools the anger and reveals his real need.

passage: My name's Ramesh, and last month I was sure my sister's husband, Nitin, was trying to take over her wedding anniversary party. He kept changing the menu, booking the hall without asking, calling the decorator himself. I told my wife he was a control freak who wanted all the praise. I was hot about it for days. Then one night, lying awake, I asked myself a strange question: am I doing the same thing? I'd been planning the surprise slideshow for weeks, and I hadn't told anyone because I wanted it to be my moment. It stung, but it was true. What I really wanted was to be included, not to control Nitin. The next day I called him. "Can I help with anything? And can I show a slideshow?" He sounded relieved. "Please! I'm drowning."

qa.q: What was Ramesh secretly planning for the party?
qa.a: A surprise slideshow.

qa.q: Why did asking "am I doing the same thing?" sting for Ramesh?
qa.a: Ramesh felt ashamed to see that the wish for control and praise blamed on Nitin was also inside Ramesh, in the secret slideshow.

qa.q: What did Ramesh discover about what was really needed, and how was it met?
qa.a: Ramesh really wanted to be included; calling Nitin to offer help and ask about the slideshow met that need.

qa.q: How did Nitin seem to feel when Ramesh called?
qa.a: Nitin sounded relieved and overwhelmed, suggesting he was struggling with the work, not trying to grab control.

grounding: Shows an adult sure of a relative's selfish motives pausing to ask whether the same impulse exists in themselves, easing the heat and finding the real need.

passage:
Supervisor's note, product team, Wednesday.
Eshaan came to our weekly check-in angry. "Amandeep is avoiding me on purpose. She won't answer my messages. She wants me to fail the launch." I asked for examples. He had two unanswered messages, both sent late at night. I asked one question: "Have you been avoiding her at all?" He was quiet for a while. Then he admitted he hadn't shared his design drafts with her for two weeks, because he was afraid she'd get the credit. He said, "I've been doing exactly what I'm blaming her for." His shoulders dropped. We talked about what he actually needs: clear ownership of the design work. What I did next: I set up a short meeting with both of them on Friday to split the launch tasks in writing.

qa.q: How many unanswered messages did Eshaan have?
qa.a: Two, both sent late at night.

qa.q: Why did Eshaan's shoulders drop after answering the question?
qa.a: Eshaan felt relieved and a little ashamed once he saw he had been avoiding Amandeep himself, so the anger lost its heat.

qa.q: Why is splitting the launch tasks in writing a good next step?
qa.a: It meets Eshaan's real need for clear ownership, so neither person has to guard their work from the other.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have seen the last two weeks?
qa.a: Amandeep may have felt shut out of the design drafts and been unaware that Eshaan thought she was avoiding him.

grounding: Shows an adult certain of a colleague's bad motives pausing to find the same impulse in himself, which reveals what he actually needs.

Thursday, late.

All afternoon I was sure Seema wanted my project. She kept copying the director on my emails, asked for my client notes "just to read", and smiled too much in the review. I typed a sharp message to her twice and deleted it twice.

On the bus home I asked myself the annoying question: have I ever wanted her work? Yes. Last month, when she got the launch, I read her whole deck looking for mistakes. That is exactly what I was accusing her of.

Writing that down made my chest loosen. What I actually want is for the director to see my work, not to beat Seema. So tomorrow I'll ask the director for ten minutes, and I'll tell Seema plainly that I'd like my name on the client notes.

Vandana

qa.q: How many times did Vandana type and delete a sharp message to Seema?
qa.a: Vandana typed the sharp message twice and deleted it twice.

qa.q: Why did Vandana feel so certain that Seema wanted the project?
qa.a: Vandana was anxious about being overlooked and had once wanted Seema's launch too, so seeing that same wish in Seema felt obvious.

qa.q: What small step cooled Vandana down, and what comes next?
qa.a: Asking whether the same wish lived in Vandana took the heat out; next come a calm ten minutes with the director and a direct request to Seema about the notes.

qa.q: How might Seema have experienced the next day if the sharp message had been sent?
qa.a: Seema would likely feel accused and defensive over ordinary questions, and the two would argue instead of sorting out credit.

grounding: Shows an adult, sure of Seema's bad motives, who spots the same wish in themself and finds the real need is to be seen by the director.

passage:
The kasba market was closing when Tanvir saw the new board outside Amandeep's shop: mustard oil, five rupees less. His jaw tightened. "He wants me finished," he told his wife Rukhsana, stacking tins louder than needed. "Twenty years side by side, and now this."

Rukhsana said nothing, only handed him tea. On the step he turned the thought over. Last Diwali, when Amandeep's supplier was late, hadn't Tanvir himself quietly hoped those customers would drift over for good? He had even moved his sweets to the front.

He gave one sheepish laugh, and the anger thinned. He did not want to crush anyone. He wanted to know the old customers would keep coming. Next morning he walked across with two glasses of tea and asked Amandeep where the cheaper oil came from.

qa.q: What did Amandeep's new board advertise?
qa.a: Mustard oil, five rupees less.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir feel so sure that Amandeep wanted to finish him?
qa.a: Tanvir was worried about losing customers and had once quietly hoped Amandeep's buyers would drift over, so that same wish felt like the obvious motive.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Walking over with tea and asking about the oil worked, because it turned a suspicion into a plain conversation between neighbours.

qa.q: How might Rukhsana have seen Tanvir's anger that evening?
qa.a: Rukhsana likely noticed the loud stacking and chose quiet and tea, trusting Tanvir to cool down before talking.

grounding: Shows a shopkeeper who, sure a neighbour is out to ruin him, recalls wishing the same and finds his real need is steady customers.

passage: In the open-plan office in Prague, Vera watched Emil present the project update to the director and felt her face burn. He's trying to take the credit, she thought. He always does. She was already drafting a sharp message in her head. Then she stopped, coffee halfway to her lips, and asked herself the question her old mentor used to ask: is any of this in me? The answer came fast and uncomfortable. She wanted the director to notice her. She had wanted to present it herself. Emil had simply been asked. The heat drained out of her. She didn't send the message. Instead she asked her manager for a chance to present the next phase.

qa.q: Where did this happen?
qa.a: In the open-plan office in Prague.

qa.q: What did Vera feel as Emil presented?
qa.a: Her face burned; she felt angry and certain he was stealing credit, until she saw her own wish to be noticed.

qa.q: What did Vera's question change?
qa.a: Asking "is any of this in me?" revealed her own wish for credit, took the heat out, and led her to ask for what she actually needed, a chance to present.

qa.q: What would have changed for Emil if Vera had sent the sharp message?
qa.a: He would have been accused of something he hadn't done, since he had simply been asked, and their working relationship would suffer.

grounding: An adult certain that a colleague is grabbing credit pauses to see the same wish in herself, which cools her and shows what she needs.

passage: In the staff meeting at the Darjeeling school, Dolma suggested a new reading programme, and Rashmi felt certain: she's doing this to make me look lazy. Rashmi's fingers tightened around her pen. She almost said something cutting about Dolma "always needing attention". Then she paused and wrote in the margin of her notes: What part of this is mine? She looked at the words for a while. The truth was that Rashmi had wanted to propose a reading club herself, and had been quietly comparing herself with Dolma all term. The motive she felt so strongly wasn't Dolma's; it was her own. After the meeting she went up to Dolma. "I had a similar idea. Could we plan it together?" Dolma's face lit up.

qa.q: What did Rashmi write in the margin?
qa.a: "What part of this is mine?"

qa.q: What did Rashmi feel when Dolma made her suggestion?
qa.a: She felt threatened and angry, certain Dolma was trying to make her look lazy.

qa.q: What did the pause reveal, and what did Rashmi do with it?
qa.a: It showed Rashmi had been comparing herself and wanted to propose the idea too; she turned that into an offer to plan it together.

qa.q: How did Dolma respond to Rashmi's offer?
qa.a: Her face lit up; she seemed happy and relieved to have a partner rather than a rival.

grounding: An adult certain about a colleague's bad motive asks what part is her own, and finds her own competitiveness and need.

passage:
So, the Bidisha story. Okay. Last spring Bidisha got the lead on the big client pitch, and I was sure she'd got it by sweet-talking our manager. Not suspicious, certain. I had a whole theory. At eleven at night I was drafting a message to HR.
Then I stopped and asked myself, out loud, like an idiot in my kitchen: "Jasleen, is any of this in you?" And, yeah. I'd been hoping someone would notice me without my having to ask. Saying that took all the heat out.
What I actually needed wasn't to expose Bidisha. It was to tell my manager I wanted to lead the next one. So I did, the next morning, and she just said, "Why didn't you say so earlier?" Bidisha and I are fine now. I even asked her how she prepared.

qa.q: What was Jasleen drafting at eleven at night?
qa.a: A message to HR.

qa.q: Why did the certainty about Bidisha feel so strong to Jasleen?
qa.a: Jasleen felt jealous and overlooked, and that unspoken wish to be noticed made Bidisha's success look like scheming.

qa.q: What step took the heat out, and what came next?
qa.a: Pausing to ask whether the same impulse was inside; naming it showed the real need, so Jasleen asked the manager to lead the next pitch instead of sending the message.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have been affected if the message to HR had been sent?
qa.a: She could have faced an unfair accusation and felt hurt and distrustful, and the working relationship might never have recovered.

grounding: An adult sure of a colleague's bad motives asks what part of it is theirs, which cools the anger and shows what they really need.
